opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so outreach for singular learning theory has been an interesting challenge, because the theory itself comes out of some pretty heavy mathematics: algebraic geometry, resolution of singularities, empirical process theory. If you lead with that, you lose almost everyone, including a lot of the alignment researchers we most want to reach.

So the way I've come to approach it is to start from the questions people already care about and work backwards to the math. The pitch isn't "here's a beautiful theory of Bayesian statistics." It's "we don't understand why neural networks generalize, we don't understand how structure forms during training, and here's a framework that makes specific claims about both." Once people see that the geometry of the loss landscape, especially the degenerate, singular parts, actually tells you something about what a model learns and when, they get curious about the machinery.

A big part of it has also been finding the right intermediate level of explanation. There's a very rigorous level, which is Watanabe's books, and there's a very hand-wavy level, which is "flat minima generalize better." A lot of what we've tried to do is build a middle layer: the learning coefficient as a measure of effective complexity, the idea that the posterior concentrates around singularities, and that phase transitions in learning correspond to moving between regions with different tradeoffs between loss and complexity. You can convey a lot of that with pictures and simple examples before anyone has to touch a blow-up.

Then there's the community side. Early on that meant things like the summit we organized, writing distillations on LessWrong, recording lecture series, and just talking to people one-on-one. Over time I've become more convinced that the most persuasive outreach is empirical results. If you can show that a quantity like the local learning coefficient tracks developmental stages in a transformer, or picks out when a model forms an induction circuit, that does more than any number of explainer posts. People take the theory seriously once it starts predicting things they can check.

I also try to be honest about what the theory doesn't yet do. Its classical results are asymptotic and Bayesian, and real networks are trained with SGD on finite data, so there are real gaps to bridge. I think being upfront about that builds more trust than overselling, and it invites people to help close those gaps rather than dismiss the whole thing.

r001.rationale: The response says to start from questions people already care about and work back to the math, but does not clearly describe tailoring outreach to individual researchers’ agendas.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that outreach has been a bit of a two-pronged thing for us. On the one hand, singular learning theory is genuinely a very mathematical subject. It comes out of algebraic geometry, Bayesian statistics, Watanabe's work going back a couple of decades, and if you try to communicate it faithfully, you very quickly end up talking about resolution of singularities and the real log canonical threshold, and most people, understandably, check out at that point. So part of the job has just been translation: figuring out what the core intuitions are and trying to express them in language that a machine learning researcher, or an alignment researcher, can actually do something with.

The way I usually frame it is something like: classical learning theory assumes your model is "regular," meaning the map from parameters to functions is nice and locally one-to-one, and that's just false for neural networks. There are huge degenerate regions in parameter space where lots of different parameters compute the same function. And it turns out that degeneracy isn't a bug, it's basically the whole story. It controls generalization, it controls what the posterior concentrates on, and SLT gives you a quantity, the learning coefficient, that measures that degeneracy and acts as a kind of effective dimension or complexity. Once people have that picture, a lot of the rest follows, and you don't need to have read the textbook to get there.

The other prong has been much more hands-on. Early on, we ran things like the SLT summer school and the workshops at Timaeus, and the goal there wasn't really to produce more theorists. It was to get people who already work with real models to pick up the tools and try them. Because I think the thing that actually convinces people isn't a proof, it's seeing the local learning coefficient track phase transitions in a transformer during training, or seeing it pick up on structure that loss curves don't show you. That's the moment where it stops being abstract.

And I'd say the third thing, which is less about outreach and more about epistemics, is being very upfront about what we don't yet know. There's a temptation when you're excited about a framework to oversell it, and SLT has a bunch of open problems: the theory is cleanest in the Bayesian setting and we train with SGD, the estimators are approximate, a lot of the interpretability claims are still speculative. I think the community has been more receptive precisely because we try to say, here's what the theory actually establishes, here's what's an empirical bet, and here's where we might be wrong. That's just better science, but it also builds trust in a way that hype doesn't.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes translating SLT’s intuitions and offering hands-on workshops, but does not say outreach is personalized around questions in other researchers’ agendas that SLT could help answer.

astra-6.text:
I try to start with the questions people already care about, rather than with the mathematical machinery. Why do these models generalize? What changes during training? What would it mean to measure the complexity of the solution a network has actually learned? Then singular learning theory becomes a possible way of making progress on those questions.

There are different levels to that conversation. You can give an intuition for why counting parameters is a poor measure of complexity without introducing algebraic geometry. If someone wants to understand where the results come from, then you can go deeper into the mathematics.

And I think it’s important to distinguish what the theory establishes from what we hope it will help us understand about neural networks. You want people to be excited enough to investigate it, but also to see where the assumptions and open questions are.

r001.rationale: The response says to start from questions people already care about, but it does not clearly describe tailoring outreach to questions on other researchers’ agendas.

sol-6.1.text:
I try to start with the questions people already care about. If you’re working on interpretability or trying to understand how a model changes during training, I want to explain what singular learning theory might let you say about that. The mathematical machinery can come later, once there’s a reason to be interested.

And I think it’s important to distinguish the established theory from the things we’re hoping it can help us understand about neural networks. There’s a lot of promise there, but I’d rather give people a concrete example they can interrogate than ask them to buy into a whole framework.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to start with questions people already care about, such as interpretability or how models change during training, and explain what singular learning theory could help answer.
